Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)
- Assessment summary: Adult patient with 6 weeks of intermittent left-sided hearing difficulty with unilateral tinnitus and mild imbalance (no true vertigo, minimal nausea). No ear pain, no discharge, afebrile. Right ear perceived normal. Similar brief episode ~1 year ago. No examination yet via video.
- Clinical reasoning consistent with transcript and DDx:
  - First priority is to exclude conductive causes such as cerumen impaction via otoscopy (as discussed).
  - If ear canal/eardrum are normal, consider inner ear/balance system causes. DDx includes Meniere disease (fluctuating unilateral symptoms with tinnitus and imbalance) and less likely retrocochlear pathology (e.g., vestibular schwannoma) given short time course and age.
  - Eustachian tube dysfunction/otitis media with effusion is also possible but less supported without aural fullness or URI/allergy history.
- No contradictions identified between transcript and DDx.

Management Plan
- Face-to-face clinic appointment in 4–5 days for otoscopic examination to rule out wax/physical blockage and assess middle/inner ear concerns.
- Provide and review tinnitus educational leaflet prior to visit to inform discussion of management options if ear exam is normal.
- Safety net: Not an emergency. If symptoms worsen or new symptoms develop (e.g., severe vertigo, neurological deficits, severe ear pain, discharge), patient to seek earlier care or book another appointment/video review.
- Follow-up: Clinic will contact/slot patient; support number provided to arrange appointment.

Consider:
- Pathology tests as above: Not recorded.
- EPC referral for allied health (10x visits/year): Not recorded.
- Dental referral: Not recorded.
- Optometry referral: Not recorded.
- Audiometry referral: Not recorded.
- Dietitian referral: Not recorded.
- CTG registration (if not enrolled): Not recorded.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
- Cerumen impaction (Moderate): Common, painless cause of unilateral conductive hearing loss and tinnitus; aligns with clinician plan to exclude with otoscopy.
- Meniere disease (Moderate): Fluctuating unilateral hearing symptoms with tinnitus and episodic imbalance; lack of true spinning vertigo/aural fullness lowers classic fit but remains plausible.
- Vestibular schwannoma (Low): Unilateral hearing loss with tinnitus and imbalance can indicate retrocochlear pathology; less likely due to short 6-week time course and younger age; consider only if persistent/progressive or if audiometry/otoscopy suggest sensorineural pattern.
